Clause 6.3 versus 6.4: answering the "which clause" question

If a procedure or an assistant answer cites "clause 6.3" for external intervals in sour service, check the edition. In API 510, eleventh edition, 6.3 is the RBI clause and the default external interval rule is 6.4.1. Neither clause contains a sour-specific number. The question usually comes from mixing up the RBI route with the default ceilings.

The distinction matters in an audit. A plan that says "external every five years per 6.3" is citing the wrong clause, because 6.3 is what lets an owner move away from the five-year default, not what sets it. Under the eleventh edition, an RBI-based external interval may exceed five years but is capped at ten. A plan that relies on 6.3 should show the RBI assessment, its API RP 580 basis, and the engineer and inspector approval cycle. If your site still works to an older edition through a jurisdictional adoption, numbering may differ; confirm against the edition your program cites.

Similar-service and multizone shortcuts that sour service also closes

Beyond 6.5.2.1 b) 6), the eleventh edition closes a second shortcut that operators of vessel trains often rely on. Under 6.5.3, the results of an internal inspection on one vessel can normally support on-stream substitution on a similar vessel in the same or similar service. The same clause says that if the vessel is subject to environmental cracking or hydrogen damage, those similar-service results cannot be used that way.

In practice, this hits trains of sour water drums, amine contactors, flash drums and overhead accumulators that are identical in design and service. Internally inspecting the worst-case vessel and crediting the others is a common and legitimate practice for thinning mechanisms. For wet H2S vessels, each vessel needs its own internal inspection or its own RBI case under 6.5.2.2. Cracking depends heavily on local factors such as weld hardness, residual stress, plate cleanliness and local water chemistry, which can differ between vessels that look identical on paper.

Clause 6.5.4 lets a large vessel with zones of different corrosion rates treat each zone separately for intervals and for on-stream substitution. For sour service, the logic runs the same way. If only the lower section of a column sees free water with dissolved H2S, the inspection plan can concentrate crack-capable examination there. The damage-mechanism review must justify the zone boundary, and the boundary should be revisited whenever process conditions change. A zone that is "dry" in normal operation can see condensation during start-up, shutdown or upsets.

Wet hydrogen versus high-temperature hydrogen: two different questions

One common phrasing asks about "wet hydrogen service" and whether API 510 treats hydrogen damage as a separate mechanism. API 510 lists hydrogen-related damage in several separate places in 5.4.1. Wet H2S damage (blistering, HIC, SOHIC, SSC) is low-temperature damage driven by aqueous corrosion. High-temperature hydrogen attack sits elsewhere in the list, with reference to API RP 941, and hydrogen embrittlement is listed as a metallurgical change.

The inspection consequences differ:

DamageDriverReference the code points toInspection implication
Wet H2S damage (blistering, HIC, SOHIC, SSC)Atomic hydrogen from sulfide corrosion in free water, at low to moderate temperatureAPI RP 571Crack-capable surface and volumetric NDE; on-stream substitution normally lost
High-temperature hydrogen attack (HTHA)Hydrogen at elevated temperature and partial pressure reacting with carbides in steelAPI RP 571 and API RP 941Specialised advanced UT techniques; susceptibility screening against the operating envelope
Hydrogen embrittlementLoss of ductility from absorbed hydrogen, often seen during cool-down or in high-strength materialsAPI RP 571Managed through materials, start-up and shutdown practice, and crack detection at susceptible locations

All three count as "hydrogen damage" for the purposes of condition 6 in 6.5.2.1 b). A hydroprocessing reactor effluent drum may face both HTHA and wet H2S damage in different zones. Its inspection plan must name both and match a technique to each. See the companion guide to high temperature hydrogen attack and API RP 941 for the high-temperature side.

Regulatory overlay: OSHA PSM and offshore 30 CFR 250

API 510 becomes mandatory when a regulator or jurisdiction adopts it, and two federal regimes matter most for sour vessels. OSHA's process safety management standard requires mechanical integrity inspections that follow recognised and generally accepted good engineering practice. BSEE's offshore production safety rule requires pressure vessels on Outer Continental Shelf production facilities to be repaired, maintained and inspected in accordance with API 510.

OSHA 29 CFR 1910.119(j)(4). For covered processes, inspection and testing procedures must follow recognised and generally accepted good engineering practices (RAGAGEP). Their frequency must be consistent with manufacturers' recommendations and good engineering practice, and more frequent if prior operating experience shows it is needed. For refinery and gas-plant pressure vessels, API 510 is the usual RAGAGEP. The "more frequent" language matters in sour service. A documented history of HIC or SSC findings in a unit is the kind of operating experience that can require shorter intervals than the API 510 ceiling, and auditors look for evidence that the program responded to its own findings. See OSHA PSM mechanical integrity programs and the background on HIC and SOHIC sour cracking.

30 CFR 250.851 (offshore and offshore-adjacent assets). BSEE's requirements table for pressure and fired vessels supporting production operations requires them to be designed, fabricated and code stamped to the applicable ASME sections, and to be repaired, maintained and inspected in accordance with API 510. This is where questions about "30 CFR alignment for offshore-adjacent assets" usually land. For a vessel inside BSEE jurisdiction, API 510 is not optional, and the environmental-cracking condition on on-stream substitution comes along with it. Two practical points follow:

  • API 510 Section 9 gives alternative rules for exploration and production vessels, as the guide above explains. Whether a given offshore vessel is inspected under Section 6 or Section 9 should be stated in the operator's inspection program and confirmed with BSEE for that facility. Do not assume one or the other.
  • Onshore facilities next to offshore operations (receiving terminals, gas plants and shore bases) usually fall under OSHA PSM and state rules rather than BSEE. Mapping each vessel to its regulator is part of the inspection program, and the answer can differ for vessels on the same site.

State boiler and pressure vessel programs add a third layer for some vessels. Many states reference the National Board Inspection Code and some accept owner-user inspection programs. Confirm with your jurisdiction. See API 510 vs the NBIC commissioned inspector and the NBIC (NB-23) overview.

Canada: sour service under provincial programs

Sour gas processing is common in Alberta and northeast British Columbia, and pressure vessels there are regulated provincially, not by API 510 alone. In Alberta, ABSA administers the pressure equipment regulations and approves owner-user inspection programs. API 510 is widely used within those programs for refinery and gas-plant vessels, but the regulator and the approved quality management system set intervals, inspector qualifications and reporting. Ontario's TSSA and other provincial authorities work on similar principles, generally adopting CSA B51.

The engineering logic in the guide above still applies. Sour vessels need crack-capable NDE, and thickness-based remaining life does not date cracking. The compliance route, though, is provincial. Confirm with the provincial regulator and your approved program.

A worked example: planning the internal inspection of a sour drum

Take a carbon steel sour water stripper feed drum with a negligible general corrosion rate and a long remaining life. Thinning arithmetic gives a comfortable ceiling, so the ten-year cap governs. Because the drum handles wet H2S, the next inspection is internal unless an RBI case under 6.5.2.2 supports on-stream inspection. The questions that matter are what the internal inspection must cover and how to stage it within the turnaround.

A qualitative planning sequence that inspection teams commonly use:

  1. Confirm the damage mechanism review. Which wet H2S forms are credible, where free water collects, the vessel's PWHT history and any hardness data. If the review is older than the last process change, update it first; 6.2.2.1 requires intervals to be re-established when service conditions change.
  2. Set examination scope by mechanism. SSC and surface-breaking SOHIC: WFMT on internal welds and heat-affected zones after abrasive or water-jet cleaning, at the coverage the plan specifies. HIC and blistering: visual for bulges plus straight-beam UT or phased array scanning of shell and head plate in wetted zones. Subsurface SOHIC at welds: angle-beam UT, phased array or TOFD.
  3. Plan surface preparation and access. WFMT sensitivity depends on cleaning. Scaffolding, blasting and lighting have to be scheduled before the NDE crew arrives, and the plan should say who verifies surface condition before examination.
  4. Decide in advance what happens if cracking is found. Clause 5.10.3 requires crack-like flaws and environmental cracking to be assessed by the inspector together with an engineer or corrosion specialist, referring to API 579-1/ASME FFS-1. Have the sizing method (depth and length) agreed beforehand so the data is usable for that assessment.
  5. Record coverage, not just results. The next interval depends on what was examined. A report that states the percentage of weld length and wetted area examined, by method, supports the next decision; "no relevant indications" without coverage does not.

Any change to the interval after the inspection, whether shorter because of findings or longer through RBI, is the owner's decision under the code, made by the inspector and engineer within the owner-operator's quality assurance system.

Examiner qualification and procedure control

API 510 is specific about who performs NDE and what records the inspector needs. Clause 4.5 says the examiner does not need API 510 certification or to be the owner's employee, but must be trained and competent in the procedures used. The owner may require certifications such as ASNT SNT-TC-1A, ASNT CP-189, CGSB or AWS QC1. The examiner's employer must keep certification records and make them available to the inspector.

For sour service this goes beyond paperwork. WFMT on prepared welds, phased array scanning for HIC and SOHIC, and TOFD sizing are all technique-sensitive. Before the turnaround, the inspector should be able to see:

  • written procedures for each method, reviewed by a Level III, stating surface preparation, equipment, calibration, scan plans and reporting thresholds;
  • certifications for each technician in the method and level used, issued under the contractor's written practice;
  • for advanced UT, a scan plan or technique sheet showing coverage of the welds and zones the inspection plan names;
  • a clear statement of what each technique can and cannot detect in that geometry, which is the "effectiveness" evidence 6.5.2.2 asks for when RBI is used to justify on-stream inspection.

Common mistakes that undermine a sour vessel interval

  • Crediting similar-service results across a train of sour vessels. Clause 6.5.3 does not allow this for vessels subject to environmental cracking or hydrogen damage.
  • Treating a "dry" zone as permanently dry. Start-up, shutdown and upset conditions can wet zones that are dry in normal operation. Multizone treatment under 6.5.4 needs that justification.
  • Citing 6.3 as the source of a five-year external interval. The default rule is 6.4.1; 6.3 is the RBI route.
  • Specifying "MT" without saying wet fluorescent or stating surface preparation. The method description in the plan should match the sensitivity the mechanism needs.
  • Reporting findings without coverage. The next interval depends on what was examined as much as on what was found.
  • Not re-running the review after a feed or process change. New crudes, added wash water or changes in cyanide levels can change wet H2S severity. Clause 6.2.2.1 and the site's management-of-change process both apply.

How Atlantis supports sour-service vessel programs

Atlantis performs the NDE that API 510 inspection plans require for wet H2S vessels and delivers results to the owner's API 510 authorized inspector, who remains inspector of record and sets intervals. Further questions on sour-service intervals

How does API 510 interact with 30 CFR 250 for offshore-adjacent assets?

For production facilities on the Outer Continental Shelf, 30 CFR 250.851 requires pressure and fired vessels to be repaired, maintained and inspected in accordance with API 510, which brings its intervals and on-stream conditions into the federal requirement. Onshore vessels next to offshore operations usually fall under OSHA PSM and state rules instead. Confirm each vessel's regulator.

Can one internal inspection cover a train of identical sour drums?

Not for on-stream substitution. API 510 6.5.3 says similar-service results cannot be used to substitute on-stream for internal inspection when the vessel is subject to environmental cracking or hydrogen damage.

Does OSHA PSM require shorter intervals for sour vessels?

OSHA 1910.119(j)(4) requires inspection frequency consistent with good engineering practice and more frequent inspection if prior operating experience shows it is necessary. Documented cracking history in sour service can be that kind of experience.

Is HTHA treated the same way as wet H2S damage in API 510?

Both count as hydrogen damage for the on-stream substitution condition, but they are separate mechanisms in 5.4.1 with different references (API RP 941 for HTHA) and different inspection techniques.

Who performs the NDE on a sour vessel, and who decides the interval?

Qualified examiners perform the NDE under the owner's specifications. API 510 does not require them to hold API 510 certification. The interval is set by the inspector or engineer under the owner-operator's quality assurance system.

Have a sour vessel coming due? Ask for an NDE scope and quote or ask about PAUT and TOFD for HIC and SOHIC.
